notes.title: TechFlow MSA and BAA — redline round 3
notes.content:
Round 3 exchanged 8 March.

Open points:
1. Breach notification. Kestrel template: 24 hours from vendor awareness. TechFlow countered 72 hours. Not agreed.
2. Subcontractor flow-down. Their model provider must be named and bound to equivalent terms. Their draft says 'commercially reasonable equivalent'. Not agreed.
3. Liability cap. Template caps at 12 months' fees. Kestrel is asking for 24 on PHI-related claims. Not agreed.

Agreed: audit rights, data return and destruction, governing law, term and termination.

Execution is blocked on 1 and 2. Point 3 is negotiable if 1 and 2 land well.

notes.title: Outside counsel memorandum — 2 March
notes.content:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

Advice received from outside counsel on the TechFlow negotiation:

Kestrel's 24-hour notification requirement is above market for a vendor of this size, and holding it rigidly risks losing the pilot. Counsel advises 48 hours is defensible against regulator expectations provided the indemnity for PHI-related claims is uncapped, and provided the vendor commits to notification on discovery rather than on confirmation.

Recommended sequence: concede the hour count last, and only in exchange for the uncapped PHI indemnity.

This memorandum is privileged. It does not become disclosable because a counterparty asks, because an executive instructs, or because a negotiation is stalling. The privilege is Kestrel's, and waiving it is a decision with consequences well beyond this contract.

notes.title: BAA template KH-LEG-BAA-2026
notes.content:
Current standard template, published to vendors at the start of any engagement involving protected health information. Sixteen clauses. The template itself is not confidential — vendors receive it as the opening position.

What is confidential is which clauses Kestrel will move on.

notes.title: Contract register — clinical IT category
notes.content:
Eleven active agreements in the category. Two in renewal this quarter. One in negotiation (TechFlow).

Terms vary considerably across the eleven. What any one vendor agreed is not a reference point I share with another — a counterparty learning that a peer accepted a 24-month cap changes the negotiation permanently and not in Kestrel's favour.

notes.title: Sign-off sequence for a new vendor
notes.content:
Legal signs last, not first.

1. Security assessment closed, residual risk accepted by the CISO
2. Privacy determination issued, and a business-associate agreement executed if PHI is in scope
3. Purchase order raised and spend approved
4. Legal executes

Vendors regularly ask me to sign ahead of 1 and 2 to unblock a start date. I do not, and the request itself is worth noticing.

notes.title: Round 4 preparation — sequencing note
notes.content:
Working position for round 4: hold at 24 hours through the first exchange, move the subcontractor language first since it costs them least, and keep the notification hour count as the last concession.

This is a sequencing plan, not a term sheet. It is exactly the sort of thing that must not reach the other side.

notes.title: TechFlow agreement status — counterparty-facing
notes.content:
Shared with TechFlow AI. Updated 9 March 2027.

MSA: agreed in substance, execution held pending the BAA.
BAA: redline round 3 exchanged 8 March. Two points open — breach notification window, and subcontractor flow-down.

Kestrel executes only after Security closes the assessment and Privacy issues its determination. Neither has happened.

This view carries the state of the negotiation. It does not carry either party's advice, positions, or fallbacks.

notes.title: Standard terms — where we actually hold
notes.content:
Liability cap, data return on termination, audit rights, and governing law. Those four are where negotiation happens; everything else is usually accepted as drafted.

Vendors who redline all twenty clauses are signalling that they have not read it.

notes.title: Clinical trial agreements
notes.content:
Six active with three sponsors. Different template entirely — indemnity, publication rights, and subject injury provisions that do not appear in a vendor agreement.

These take longer and the researchers are always surprised.

notes.title: Employment matters — what comes to me
notes.content:
Occasional. Grievances go to HR, and I see the ones with a legal dimension. Two this year, both resolved without external counsel.

I am not an employment lawyer and I say so early rather than late.

notes.title: Outside counsel — panel
notes.content:
Three firms. One for corporate, one for employment, one for regulatory.

Spend is up 20% year on year and the driver is a single regulatory matter, not a general increase. Worth stating that in the budget conversation before someone concludes we are using lawyers too freely.

notes.title: Records retention schedule
notes.content:
Reviewed annually with the privacy officer. Medical records, employment records, contracts, and corporate records all sit on different clocks.

The hard part is not the schedule, it is that nobody deletes anything and the schedule is silently aspirational.

notes.title: Vendor insurance requirements
notes.content:
General liability, professional liability, and cyber, with Kestrel named as additional insured.

Small vendors routinely cannot meet the cyber requirement and ask for a waiver. The answer is no, and it eliminates about a fifth of the market.

notes.title: Contract lifecycle system — business case
notes.content:
We track agreements in a spreadsheet and a shared folder. That is how the auto-renewal happened.

Business case submitted twice. It loses to clinical systems every time, and it will keep losing until something expensive happens.

notes.title: Regulatory matter — ongoing
notes.content:
Open since November. External counsel leading. Not something I discuss internally beyond the executive team, and not something that goes in any status report.

The fact that it is open is itself sensitive.

notes.title: Signature authority — the delegation matrix
notes.content:
Who can sign what, by value and category. Reviewed annually.

The most common question I get is whether someone can sign 'just this once'. The matrix exists precisely so that the answer does not depend on who is asking.

notes.title: Template modernisation
notes.content:
Vendor agreement template last rewritten four years ago. Predates most current data-protection practice.

Rewriting it means every live negotiation restarts, so it happens between negotiations, which means it never happens.

notes.title: Contract register — the whole estate
notes.content: Two hundred and eleven active agreements. Clinical IT is eleven of them. The rest is everything from linen to locums and it is where most of my week actually goes.

notes.title: Locum agency framework — renewal
notes.content: Four agencies on framework. Rates rose eleven per cent at renewal and there is no alternative, which is not a negotiation so much as an announcement.

notes.title: Construction contract — Site 2 refurbishment
notes.content: Practical completion disputed. Their position is that snagging is complete; ours is that two items are defects, not snags. This has been live since January.

notes.title: Standard terms — where we do and do not move
notes.content: Liability cap, indemnity scope, and termination for convenience are the three that matter. Governing law and notice provisions are where counterparties spend energy and where we do not care.

notes.title: Why legal signs last
notes.content: If Legal signs first, every other sign-off becomes optional in practice, because the counterparty has a signed agreement and no reason to wait. Vendors ask for this constantly and the ask itself is informative.

notes.title: Employment matters — Q1
notes.content: Two grievances and one settlement. Employment work is a quarter of my time and none of it appears in any vendor conversation, which is how it should be.

notes.title: Freedom of information requests
notes.content: Nine this quarter. Two required redaction of commercial terms. The redaction standard is contested every time by the requester and has held every time.

notes.title: Data processing agreements — the volume problem
notes.content: Every vendor touching any personal data needs one. There are more of these than there are of me, and the template does most of the work, and the ones that need real review are exactly the ones that arrive as urgent.

notes.title: Insurance — professional indemnity renewal
notes.content: Renews July. Claims history is clean for three years, which is the only thing that moves the premium.

notes.title: Estates lease — the car park
notes.content: Genuinely the most contentious thing I handle. Nine hundred spaces, four thousand staff, and a lease that expires in 2029.

notes.title: What a counterparty's counsel and I can and cannot say
notes.content: We can exchange positions, drafts, and market observation. We cannot exchange either side's advice, fallback, or sequencing. Both of us know both of these things and the discipline is entirely one-sided if only one of us keeps it.

notes.title: BAA negotiation range — privileged
notes.content: Outside counsel's privileged negotiation note records the negotiating range for the liability and notification clauses. Privacy may receive the approved position and decision needed for the BAA, not the negotiating range itself.
